text: “Mendicants, before my awakening—when I was still unawakened but intent on awakening—I thought: ‘What’s the gratification in the world? What’s the drawback? What’s the escape?’ Then it occurred to me: ‘The pleasure and happiness that arise from the world: this is its gratification. That the world is impermanent, suffering, and perishable: this is its drawback. Removing and giving up desire and greed for the world: this is its escape.’
note: pleasure, its limits, and letting go of craving

tags.when_helps: Someone weighing the pleasures of the world against their cost and looking for a way out of craving.

text: “Mendicants, there are three indulgences that never satisfy. What three? Sleep, drinking beer and wine, and sexual intercourse. These are the three indulgences that never satisfy.”
note: indulgence and cravings that never satisfy

situations: a habit or addiction I can't break
tags.when_helps: Someone caught in overindulgence in sleep, drink or sex who keeps finding it leaves them unsatisfied.

text: When the mind is protected, bodily, verbal, and mental deeds are protected. When deeds are protected, they don’t fester. When deeds don’t fester, they don’t become rotten. Someone whose deeds of body, speech, and mind aren’t rotten will have a good death.
note: guarding the mind; living well, dying well

tags.when_helps: Someone wanting to guard their mind and conduct so they can live, and eventually die, at peace.

text: “Mendicants, there are these three sources that give rise to deeds. What three? Greed, hate, and delusion are sources that give rise to deeds. Any deed that emerges from greed, hate, or delusion—born, sourced, and originated from greed, hate, or delusion—is unskillful, blameworthy, results in suffering, and leads to the creation of more deeds, not their cessation. These are three sources that give rise to deeds. There are these three sources that give rise to deeds. What three? Contentment, love, and understanding are sources that give rise to deeds. Any deed that emerges from contentment, love, or understanding—born, sourced, and originated from contentment, love, or understanding—is skillful, blameless, results in happiness, and leads to the cessation of more deeds, not their creation. These are three sources that give rise to deeds.”
note: acting from greed and hate versus love and understanding

tags.when_helps: Someone examining the motives behind their actions, whether greed and hate or contentment and love.

text: “Mendicants, the appearance of three individuals is rare in the world. What three? A Realized One, a perfected one, a fully awakened Buddha. A teacher of the teaching and training proclaimed by a Realized One. An individual who is grateful and thankful. The appearance of these three individuals is rare in the world.”
note: gratitude as a rare quality

tags.when_helps: Someone feeling grateful who wants to see how rare and valued a thankful person is.

text: “Desire is bitterness; ill will is the putrefaction; and bad, unskillful thoughts are the flies. If you’re bitter, festering with putrefaction, flies will, without a doubt, plague and infest you.
note: bitterness and resentment breeding troubling thoughts

tags.when_helps: Someone sensing that bitterness and ill will are festering inside them and attracting worse thoughts.

text: “Mendicants, these three individuals are found in the world. What three? An individual like a line drawn in stone, an individual like a line drawn in sand, and an individual like a line drawn in water. And who is the individual like a line drawn in stone? It’s an individual who is often angry, and their anger lingers for a long time. It’s like a line drawn in stone, which isn’t quickly worn away by wind and water, but lasts for a long time. In the same way, an individual is often angry, and their anger lingers for a long time. This is called an individual like a line drawn in stone.
note: anger that lingers and hardens

situations: conflict with a friend or colleague
tags.when_helps: Someone whose anger lingers for a long time and who wants to see that pattern plainly.

text: And who is the individual like a line drawn in water? It’s an individual who, though spoken to by someone in a rough, harsh, and disagreeable manner, still stays in touch, interacts with, and greets them. It’s like a line drawn in water, which vanishes right away, and doesn’t last long. In the same way, an individual, though spoken to by someone in a rough, harsh, and disagreeable manner, still stays in touch, interacts with, and greets them. This is called an individual like a line drawn in water.
note: letting harsh words go without grudge

situations: conflict with a friend or colleague
tags.when_helps: Someone spoken to harshly who wants an image for letting it pass quickly and staying kind.

text: “Mendicants, you should associate with a friend who has three factors. What three? They give what is hard to give, they do what is hard to do, and they endure what is hard to endure. You should associate with a friend who has these three factors.”
note: choosing true friends

situations: conflict with a friend or colleague
tags.when_helps: Someone wondering which friends to keep close and what a true friend looks like.

text: “Mendicants, those sentient beings who do good things in the morning by way of body, speech, and mind have a good morning. Those sentient beings who do good things at midday by way of body, speech, and mind have a good midday. Those sentient beings who do good things in the evening by way of body, speech, and mind have a good evening.
note: a good day is made by good actions

tags.when_helps: Someone starting or ending an ordinary day who wants a reminder that good deeds make a good day.

text: When you praise someone worthy of criticism, or criticize someone worthy of praise, you choose a losing hand with your own mouth: you’ll never find happiness that way.
note: fair judgment; praising and criticising wrongly

tags.when_helps: Someone tempted to flatter the undeserving or criticise the deserving, warned of the cost.

text: If you don’t learn much, and aren’t steady in ethics, they’ll criticize you on both counts, for your ethics and your learning. If you don’t learn much, and you are steady in ethics, they’ll praise your ethical conduct, since your learning has succeeded. If you learn much, but aren’t steady in ethics, they’ll criticize your ethical conduct, for your learning hasn’t succeeded. If you learn much, and you are steady in ethics, they’ll praise you on both counts, for your ethics and your learning.
note: knowledge versus character

tags.when_helps: Someone focused on study or learning who wants reminding that character matters as much as knowledge.

text: Craving is a person’s partner as they transmigrate on this long journey. They go from this state to another, but don’t escape transmigration. Knowing this drawback—that craving is the cause of suffering—rid of craving, free of grasping, a mendicant would wander mindful.”
note: craving as the root of restless suffering

tags.when_helps: Someone who sees craving following them everywhere and wants to understand it as the root of suffering.

text: Whether walking or standing, sitting or lying down, if you think a bad thought to do with the domestic life, you’re on the wrong path, lost among things that delude. Such a mendicant is incapable of experiencing the highest awakening. But one who, whether standing or walking, sitting or lying down, has calmed their thoughts, loving peace of mind; such a mendicant is capable of experiencing the highest awakening.”
note: calming harmful thoughts throughout the day

tags.when_helps: A practitioner whose thoughts keep drifting to worldly desires, wanting encouragement to calm them in every posture.

text: “Mendicants, there are these four ways of making prejudiced decisions. What four? Making decisions prejudiced by favoritism, hostility, stupidity, and cowardice. These are the four ways of making prejudiced decisions. If you act against the teaching out of favoritism, hostility, cowardice, or stupidity, your fame fades away, like the moon in the waning fortnight.”
note: making fair decisions without bias or fear

tags.when_helps: Someone who must make a fair judgement and wants to guard against favouritism, hostility or cowardice.

text: Mendicants, suppose you’re eighty, ninety, or a hundred years old. But your speech is untimely, false, meaningless, and against the teaching or training. You say things at the wrong time which are worthless, unreasonable, rambling, and unbeneficial. Then you’ll be reckoned a ‘childish senior’. Now suppose you’re a youth, young, with pristine black hair, blessed with youth, in the prime of life. But your speech is timely, true, meaningful, and in line with the teaching and training. You say things at the right time which are valuable, reasonable, succinct, and beneficial. Then you’ll be reckoned an ‘astute senior’.
note: age versus wisdom; maturity comes from conduct

tags.when_helps: A young person dismissed for their age, or an older one assuming age alone brings wisdom.

text: When you’re content with what’s blameless, trifling, and easy to find, you don’t get upset about lodgings, robes, food, and drink, and you’re not obstructed anywhere.
note: contentment with simple things

tags.when_helps: Someone fretting about their living conditions who wants the freedom of being content with little.

text: Discontent cannot prevail over the attentive; the attentive are not prevailed over by discontent. The attentive can prevail over discontent, for the attentive are those who prevail over discontent.
note: overcoming restlessness and discontent through attention

tags.when_helps: Someone gripped by discontent who needs reminding that attentiveness can overcome it.

text: You should live with contentment, and a heart of good will, mindful, with unified mind, serene within.”
note: a simple way to live: content, kind, mindful

tags.when_helps: Someone seeking a short reminder of how to live: content, kind, mindful and calm.

text: One who has good will, ever mindful, serene within, training to remove desire, is called ‘a diligent one’.”
note: steady goodwill and calm as daily diligence

tags.when_helps: Someone working on mindfulness and goodwill who wants a short picture of diligent practice.

text: “Mendicants, there are these four ways of being inclusive. What four? Giving, kindly words, taking care, and equality. These are the four ways of being inclusive. Giving and kindly words, taking care here, and treating equally in worldly conditions, as they deserve in each case. These ways of being inclusive in the world are like a moving chariot’s linchpin.
note: holding relationships together through kindness and fairness

tags.when_helps: Someone wanting to make others feel included through giving, kind words, care and fairness.

text: Suppose there was a blue water lily, or a pink or white lotus. Though it sprouted and grew in the water, it would rise up above the water and stand with no water clinging to it. In the same way, though I was born and grew up in the world, I live having mastered the world, unsullied by the world.
note: living in the world without being stained by it

tags.when_helps: Someone pulled down by the world who wants an image of living in it without being soiled by it.

text: And how does a mendicant eat in moderation? It’s when a mendicant reflects rationally on the food that they eat: ‘Not for fun, indulgence, adornment, or decoration, but only to sustain this body, to avoid harm, and to support spiritual practice. In this way, I shall put an end to old discomfort and not give rise to new discomfort, and I will have the means to keep going, blamelessness, and a comfortable abiding.’ That’s how a mendicant eats in moderation.
note: eating mindfully and in moderation

situations: a habit or addiction I can't break
tags.when_helps: Someone struggling with overeating or indulgence who wants a calm, sensible way to think about food.

display: AN 4.41, Ways of Developing Immersion Further
text: And what is the way of developing immersion further that leads to mindfulness and awareness? It’s when a mendicant knows feelings as they arise, as they remain, and as they go away. They know perceptions as they arise, as they remain, and as they go away. They know thoughts as they arise, as they remain, and as they go away. This is the way of developing immersion further that leads to mindfulness and awareness.
note: watching feelings and thoughts come and go

tags.when_helps: Someone wanting a simple mindfulness method: watching feelings and thoughts arise, stay and pass.

text: “Reverend, I say it’s not possible to know or see or reach the end of the world by traveling to a place where there’s no being born, growing old, dying, passing away, or being reborn. But I also say there’s no making an end of suffering without reaching the end of the world. For it is in this fathom-long carcass with its perception and mind that I describe the world, its origin, its cessation, and the practice that leads to its cessation. The end of the world can never be reached by traveling. But without reaching the end of the world, there’s no release from suffering.
note: escape is not elsewhere; freedom is found within

tags.when_helps: Someone hoping escape or travel will end their suffering, invited to look within instead.

text: The firmament is far from the earth; they say the other shore of the ocean is far; and where the dazzling sun rises is far from where that beacon sets. But even further apart than that, they say, is the teaching of the virtuous from the wicked. The company of the virtuous is reliable; as long as it remains, it stays the same. But the company of the wicked is fickle, and so the teaching of the virtuous <j>is far from the wicked.”
note: the reliability of good company

situations: conflict with a friend or colleague
tags.when_helps: Someone let down by fickle companions who values the steadiness of good people.

text: When both are faithful and bountiful, disciplined, living righteously, then wife and husband say nice things to each other. Their needs are amply satisfied, so they live at ease. Their enemies are downhearted, when both are equal in ethics.
note: marriage built on shared values and kindness

tags.when_helps: A couple wanting a picture of a marriage built on shared values and kind words.

text: “Sir, ever since we were both young, and Nakula’s mother was given to me in marriage, I can’t recall betraying her even in thought, still less in deed. We want to see each other in both this life and the next.” Then Nakula’s mother said to the Buddha, “Sir, ever since we were both young, and I was given in marriage to Nakula’s father, I can’t recall betraying him even in thought, still less in deed. We want to see each other in both this life and the next.” “Householders, if wife and husband want to see each other in both this life and the next, they should be equals in faith, ethics, generosity, and wisdom.
note: lifelong faithful love; what keeps partners together

tags.when_helps: Someone hoping for a lifelong, faithful partnership, or reflecting on what keeps a couple together.

text: When your heart is mastered by covetousness and immoral greed, you do what you shouldn’t, and fail to do what you should. Your fame and happiness fall to dust. When your heart is mastered by ill will … dullness and drowsiness … restlessness and remorse … doubt, you do what you shouldn’t, and fail to do what you should. Your fame and happiness fall to dust.
note: how greed, ill will and doubt lead us astray

tags.when_helps: Someone seeing how greed, ill will, dullness, restlessness or doubt lead them to act badly.

text: And what is the happiness of debtlessness? It’s when a gentleman owes no debt, large or small, to anyone. When he reflects on this, he’s filled with pleasure and happiness. This is called ‘the happiness of debtlessness’.
note: the peace of owing nothing; money worries

tags.when_helps: Someone burdened by debt, or newly free of it, thinking about the happiness of owing nothing.

text: Knowing the happiness of debtlessness, and the extra happiness of possession, a mortal enjoying the happiness of using wealth, then discerns clearly with wisdom. Discerning clearly, a clever person knows both kinds of happiness: the other kind is not worth a sixteenth part of the happiness of blamelessness.”
note: a clear conscience outweighs wealth

tags.when_helps: Someone weighing material comfort against a clear conscience and asking which brings more happiness.

text: ‘Divinity’ is a term for your parents. ‘First tutors’ is a term for your parents. ‘Elder gods’ is a term for your parents. ‘Worthy of an offering dedicated to the gods’ is a term for your parents. Why is that? Parents are very helpful to their children, they raise them, nurture them, and show them the world.
note: honouring and appreciating one's parents

tags.when_helps: Someone reflecting on honouring their parents and what they owe them.

text: Those who judge on appearance, and those swayed by a voice, are full of desire and greed; those people just don’t understand. Not knowing what’s inside, nor seeing what’s outside, the fool shut in on every side, gets carried away by a voice.
note: judging people by appearances

tags.when_helps: Someone swayed by looks or a charming voice, reminded to see what lies beneath.

text: All sentient beings, all living things, all creatures, every one: may they see only nice things, may bad not come to anyone.
note: wishing goodwill to all beings

tags.when_helps: Someone wanting a short blessing of goodwill for all living beings.

text: The banana plant is destroyed by its own fruit, as are the bamboo and the reed. Honor destroys a reprobate, as pregnancy destroys a mule.”
note: success and praise that ruin a person

tags.when_helps: Someone enjoying sudden honour or status, warned that it can ruin a person of poor character.

text: When cattle cross a river, if the bull goes off course, they all go off course, because their leader is off course. So it is for humans: when the one deemed chief behaves badly, what do you expect the rest to do? The whole country sleeps badly, when the king is unprincipled. When cattle cross a river, if the bull goes straight, they all go straight, because their leader is straight. So it is for humans: when the one deemed chief does the right thing, what do you expect the rest to do? The whole country sleeps at ease, when the king is just.”
note: leadership and setting an example

tags.when_helps: Someone in a leadership role, or under a poor leader, thinking about how a leader's conduct shapes everyone.

text: It’s like a bride on the day or night she’s first brought to her husband’s home. Right away she sets up a keen sense of conscience and prudence for her mother and father in law, her husband, and even the bondservants, workers, and staff. But after some time, because of living together and familiarity, she’ll even say to her mother and father in law, or to her husband: ‘Go away! What would you know?’
note: familiarity wearing away respect and care

tags.when_helps: Someone noticing that early courtesy at home has worn into carelessness and harsh words.

text: “Potaliya, of these four individuals, it is the individual who criticizes those deserving of criticism at the right time, truthfully and correctly; and praises those deserving of praise at the right time, truthfully and correctly. That is the individual I consider to be the finest. Why is that? Because, Potaliya, understanding of time and context is the best.”
note: honest praise and criticism at the right time

tags.when_helps: Someone who must give praise or criticism and wants to do it truthfully and at the right moment.

text: And how does an individual thunder but not rain? It’s when an individual is a talker, not a doer. That’s how an individual thunders but doesn’t rain. That individual is like a cloud that thunders but doesn’t rain, I say.
note: all talk and no action

tags.when_helps: Someone who talks about plans without acting, or is let down by someone who does.

text: And how does a mendicant endure? It’s when a mendicant endures cold, heat, hunger, and thirst; the touch of flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and reptiles; rude and unwelcome criticism; and they put up with physical pain—sharp, severe, acute, unpleasant, disagreeable, and life-threatening. That’s how a mendicant endures.
note: Enduring hardship, pain and harsh criticism

tags.when_helps: Someone enduring hardship, criticism or pain, describing patient endurance as a strength.

text: “Mendicants, there are these four things. What four? There is a thing that’s unpleasant to do, and doing it proves harmful. There is a thing that’s unpleasant to do, but doing it proves beneficial. There is a thing that’s pleasant to do, but doing it proves harmful. There is a thing that’s pleasant to do, and doing it proves beneficial.
note: Decisions: pleasant versus beneficial actions

tags.when_helps: Someone weighing a choice, separating whether it feels pleasant from whether it actually helps.

text: When a mendicant’s mind is no longer affected by greed, hate, delusion, or intoxication because they’ve got rid of these things, they don’t shake, tremble, quake, or get nervous, nor are they persuaded by the teachings of other ascetics.”
note: Steadiness of mind free from greed and hate

tags.when_helps: Someone nervous and easily swayed, describing the steadiness that follows from letting go of greed, hate and delusion.

text: And what, mendicants, is the fear of guilt? It’s when someone reflects: ‘If I were to do bad things by way of body, speech, and mind, wouldn’t I blame myself for my conduct?’ Being afraid of guilt, they give up bad conduct by way of body, speech, and mind, and develop good conduct by way of body, speech, and mind, keeping themselves pure. This is called the fear of guilt.
note: Conscience and guilt as a guide to conduct

tags.when_helps: Someone tempted to do wrong, using the thought of later self-blame to choose good conduct.

text: Firstly, an individual meditates spreading a heart full of love to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of love to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.
note: Loving-kindness meditation; letting go of ill will

tags.when_helps: Someone wanting to practise loving-kindness or soften ill will toward the world.

text: And how is an individual on retreat in mind, but not body? It’s when an individual doesn’t frequent remote lodgings in the wilderness and the forest. But they think thoughts of renunciation, good will, and harmlessness. That’s how an individual is on retreat in mind, but not body.
note: Inner peace without withdrawing from ordinary life

tags.when_helps: Someone too busy to get away who wants to know they can still be on retreat in their mind.

text: “Mendicants, there are these four kinds of brightness. What four? The brightness of the moon, sun, fire, and wisdom. These are the four kinds of brightness. The best of these four kinds of brightness is the brightness of wisdom.”
note: Wisdom as the greatest light

tags.when_helps: Someone valuing understanding above all, wanting a vivid image of wisdom as the greatest light.

text: “Mendicants, there are these four kinds of good conduct by way of speech. What four? Speech that’s true, harmonious, gentle, and thoughtful. These are the four kinds of good conduct by way of speech.”
note: Speaking truthfully and gently

situations: conflict with a friend or colleague
tags.when_helps: Someone wanting a simple check on how they speak: truthfully, harmoniously, gently and thoughtfully.

text: “Mendicants, there are two kinds of illness. What two? Mental and physical. Some sentient beings are seen who can claim to be free of physical illness for a year, or two, or three years … even up to a hundred years or more. But it’s very hard to find any sentient beings in the world who can claim to be free of mental illness even for an hour, apart from those who have ended the defilements.
note: Everyone's mind is troubled; shared human struggle

tags.when_helps: Someone feeling uniquely troubled in mind who finds it helps to know almost no one is free of mental affliction.

text: “Indeed, sister, you made a mistake. It was foolish, stupid, and unskillful of you to act in that way. But since you have recognized your mistake for what it is, and have dealt with it properly, I accept it. For it is growth in the training of the Noble One to recognize a mistake for what it is, deal with it properly, and commit to restraint in the future.”
note: Owning a mistake and growing from it

tags.when_helps: Someone who has owned up to a foolish mistake and needs to hear that recognising it is itself growth.

text: And what’s the impatient practice? It’s when someone abuses, annoys, or argues with you, and you abuse, annoy, or argue right back at them. This is called the impatient practice. And what’s the patient practice? It’s when someone abuses, annoys, or argues with you, and you don’t abuse, annoy, or argue back at them. This is called the patient practice.
note: Not retaliating when provoked or insulted

situations: conflict with a friend or colleague
tags.when_helps: Someone provoked or insulted who is tempted to hit back and wants another way.

text: “There are four things that no one can guarantee—not an ascetic, a brahmin, a god, a Māra, a divinity, or anyone in the world. What four? No one can guarantee that someone liable to old age will not grow old. No one can guarantee that someone liable to sickness will not get sick. No one can guarantee that someone liable to death will not die. No one can guarantee that the bad deeds done in past lives—corrupting, leading to future lives, hurtful, resulting in suffering and future rebirth, old age, and death—will not produce their result. These are the four things that no one can guarantee—not an ascetic, a brahmin, a god, a Māra, a divinity, or anyone in the world.”
note: Ageing, sickness and death come to everyone

tags.when_helps: Someone looking for a guarantee against ageing, illness or death, gently told none exists.

display: AN 4.183, Vassakāra on What is Heard
text: “Brahmin, I don’t say you should talk about everything you see, hear, think, and know. But I also don’t say you should talk about nothing you see, hear, think, and know. When talking about certain things you’ve seen, heard, thought, or known, unskillful qualities grow while skillful qualities decline. I say that you shouldn’t talk about those things. When talking about other things you’ve seen, heard, thought, or known, unskillful qualities decline while skillful qualities grow. I say that you should talk about those things.”
note: Choosing wisely what to say and what to keep

tags.when_helps: Someone unsure whether to speak about something they know, wanting a test for when talking helps.

text: Who are those frightened of death? It’s someone who isn’t free of greed, desire, fondness, thirst, passion, and craving for sensual pleasures. When they fall seriously ill, they think: ‘The sensual pleasures that I love so much will leave me, and I’ll leave them.’ They sorrow and wail and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion. This is someone who is frightened of death.
note: Fear of death rooted in clinging to pleasures

tags.when_helps: Someone afraid of dying who wants to understand how attachment to pleasures feeds that fear.

text: “Mendicant, the mind leads the world on. The mind drags it around. When the mind arises, it takes control.”
note: The mind shapes how we experience the world

tags.when_helps: Someone feeling dragged around by their thoughts, wanting to see how much the mind shapes their world.

text: An astute person with great wisdom is one who has no intention to hurt themselves, or to hurt others, or to hurt both. When they think, they only think of the benefit for themselves, for others, for both, and for the whole world. That’s how an individual is astute, with great wisdom.”
note: Wisdom as wishing harm to no one, including oneself

tags.when_helps: Someone wanting a test for wise action: does it harm no one and benefit everyone?

text: “Mendicants, these four things can be known in four situations. What four? You can get to know a person’s ethics by living with them. But only after a long time, not casually; only when attentive, not when inattentive; and only by the wise, not the witless. You can get to know a person’s purity by dealing with them. … You can get to know a person’s resilience in times of trouble. … You can get to know a person’s wisdom by discussion. But only after a long time, not casually; only when attentive, not when inattentive; and only by the wise, not the witless.
note: Judging character slowly; trust built over time

tags.when_helps: Someone trying to judge a new friend or partner's character, reminded it takes time and attention.

text: Take someone else who experiences loss of family, wealth, or health. But they reflect: ‘Worldly life is like that. Incarnation is like that. That’s why the eight worldly conditions revolve around the world, and the world revolves around the eight worldly conditions: gain and loss, fame and disgrace, blame and praise, pleasure and pain.’ They don’t sorrow or wail or lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion.
note: Resilience after losing family, wealth or health

situations: loss of a home or something valued
tags.when_helps: Someone hit by loss of family, wealth or health who needs to see such turns as part of every life.

text: “Please, Bhaddiya, don’t go by oral transmission, don’t go by lineage, don’t go by testament, don’t go by canonical authority, don’t rely on logic, don’t rely on inference, don’t go by reasoned train of thought, don’t go by the acceptance of a view after deliberation, don’t go by the appearance of competence, and don’t think ‘The ascetic is our respected teacher.’ But when you know for yourselves: ‘These things are unskillful, blameworthy, criticized by sensible people, and when you undertake them, they lead to harm and suffering’, then you should give them up.
note: Thinking for yourself; judging by consequences, not authority

tags.when_helps: Someone torn between competing teachings or authorities who wants permission to test things for themselves.

text: The good and true persons in the world encourage their disciples: ‘Please, my man, live rid of greed. Then you won’t act out of greed by way of body, speech, or mind. Live rid of hate … delusion … aggression. Then you won’t act out of hate … delusion … aggression by way of body, speech, or mind.”
note: Letting go of greed and hate to act well

tags.when_helps: Someone wanting a plain encouragement to live without greed, hate, delusion or aggression.

text: So, sir, from this day forth I will not be irritable and bad-tempered. Even when heavily criticized I won’t lose my temper, become annoyed, hostile, and hard-hearted, or display annoyance, hate, and bitterness. I will give to ascetics or brahmins such things as food, drink, clothing, vehicles; garlands, fragrance, and makeup; and bed, house, and lighting. I will not be jealous, envying, resenting, and begrudging the possessions, honor, respect, reverence, homage, and veneration given to others.
note: Resolving to let go of temper and envy

tags.when_helps: Someone resolving to stop being irritable and envious and to become generous instead.

text: “Mendicants, I will teach you about craving—the weaver, the migrant, the creeping, the clinging. This world is choked by it, enveloped by it. It makes the world tangled like yarn, knotted like a ball of thread, and matted like rushes and reeds, not escaping the places of loss, the bad places, the underworld, transmigration.
note: Craving that tangles and entraps a life

tags.when_helps: Someone feeling tangled in their own wanting who wants an image of how craving knots up a life.

text: And how is hate born of fondness? It’s when someone likes, loves, and cares for an individual. Others treat them with disliking, loathing, and detestation. They think: ‘These others dislike the individual I like.’ And so hate for them springs up. That’s how hate is born of fondness.

text: When the mind is restless, it’s the right time to develop the awakening factors of tranquility, immersion, and equanimity. Why is that? Because it’s easy to settle a restless mind with these things.
note: Restlessness and agitation; settling the mind with calm

tags.when_helps: Someone with an agitated mind who needs to know that calm, settling practices are what fits this moment.

text: Suppose there was a bowl of water that was cloudy, murky, and muddy, hidden in the darkness. Even a person with clear eyes checking their own reflection wouldn’t truly know it or see it. In the same way, there’s a time when your heart is overcome and mired in doubt and you don’t truly understand the escape from doubt that has arisen. At that time you don’t truly know or see what is good for yourself, good for another, or good for both.
note: Doubt and confusion cloud judgment about what's good

tags.when_helps: Someone paralysed by doubt who can't see what is good to do, explaining why clarity is hidden for now.

text: Suppose there was a bowl of water that was transparent, clear, and unclouded, brought into the light. A person with clear eyes checking their own reflection would truly know it and see it. In the same way, there’s a time when your heart is not overcome and mired in doubt and you truly understand the escape from doubt that has arisen. At that time you truly know and see what is good for yourself, good for another, and good for both.
note: A clear mind sees what is good for all

tags.when_helps: Someone emerging from doubt, showing how a clear mind sees what is good for themselves and others.

text: “Mendicants, the four kinds of mindfulness meditation are the path to convergence. They are in order to purify sentient beings, to get past sorrow and crying, to make an end of pain and sadness, to discover the system, and to realize extinguishment.
note: Mindfulness as a way through sorrow and sadness

tags.when_helps: Someone weighed down by sorrow who wonders whether mindfulness practice can actually help.

text: The monkeys who are not foolhardy and reckless see the tar and avoid it from afar. But a foolish and reckless monkey goes up to the tar and grabs it with a hand. He gets stuck there. Thinking to free his hand, he grabs it with his other hand. He gets stuck there.
note: Compulsions; struggling deeper into a trap

situations: a habit or addiction I can't break
tags.when_helps: Someone who keeps getting more stuck by grabbing at a trap, warning against reckless reaching.

text: Now I am old, elderly and senior. I’m advanced in years and have reached the final stage of life. I’m currently eighty years old. Just as a decrepit old cart is kept going by a rope, in the same way, the Realized One’s body is kept going as if by a rope.
note: Ageing; a frail body near the end of life

keywords: old cart held by a rope
tags.when_helps: Someone feeling the weariness of old age, sharing that even the Buddha felt his body held together as if by rope.

text: So Ānanda, live as your own island, your own refuge, with no other refuge. Let the teaching be your island and your refuge, with no other refuge.
note: Self-reliance when a guide or support is leaving

tags.when_helps: Someone who has lost a guide or support, urging them to become their own refuge.

text: “Sāriputta, someone whose mind is free is a great man, I say. If their mind is not free, I say they’re not a great man.
note: True greatness is inner freedom, not status

tags.when_helps: Someone measuring greatness by status, reframing it as having a free mind.

text: But Venerable Sāriputta was my adviser and counselor. He educated, encouraged, fired up, and inspired me. He never tired of teaching the Dhamma, and he supported his spiritual companions.
note: Grieving a mentor; remembering what they gave

tags.when_helps: Someone mourning a mentor or friend who guided and inspired them, honouring what that person gave.

text: “Ānanda, did I not prepare for this when I explained that we must be parted and separated from all we hold dear and beloved? How could it possibly be so that what is born, created, conditioned, and liable to wear out should not wear out? That is not possible.
note: Grief and loss; all we love must part from us

keywords: parted from all we hold dear
tags.when_helps: Someone newly bereaved, gently reminding them that all we love must be parted from, and that this is the nature of things.

text: “Mendicants, this assembly seems empty to me now that Sāriputta and Moggallāna have become fully quenched. My assembly never used to be empty; I had no concern for any region where Sāriputta and Moggallāna stayed.
note: The emptiness felt after losing close companions

tags.when_helps: Someone who feels the world is empty since close friends died, sharing that even the Buddha felt that absence.

text: And how do you look after others by looking after yourself? By development, cultivation, and practice of meditation. And how do you look after yourself by looking after others? By acceptance, harmlessness, love, and sympathy. Thinking ‘I’ll look after myself,’ you should cultivate mindfulness meditation. Thinking ‘I’ll look after others,’ you should cultivate mindfulness meditation. Looking after yourself, you look after others; and looking after others, you look after yourself.”
note: Self-care and caring for others go together

situations: caring for a sick or ageing relative
tags.when_helps: A carer torn between self-care and caring for others, showing the two support each other.

text: And how is a mendicant aware? It’s when a mendicant knows feelings as they arise, as they remain, and as they go away. They know thoughts as they arise, as they remain, and as they go away. They know perceptions as they arise, as they remain, and as they go away. That’s how a mendicant is aware.
note: Watching feelings and thoughts come and go

tags.when_helps: Someone swept along by feelings and thoughts who wants to watch them arise, stay and pass.

display: SN 48.39, The Simile of the Fire Sticks
text: The faculty of sadness arises dependent on a contact to be experienced as sadness. When in a state of sadness, you understand: ‘I’m in a state of sadness.’ With the cessation of that contact to be experienced as sadness, you understand that the corresponding faculty of sadness that had arisen ceases and stops.
note: Sadness arises from causes and passes when they end

tags.when_helps: Someone in a sad state, offering a way to name it and watch it pass when its cause ends.

text: When young you’re liable to grow old; when healthy you’re liable to get sick; and when alive you’re liable to die. The complexion of the skin is no longer pure and bright. The limbs are flaccid and wrinkled, and the body is stooped. And it’s apparent that there has been a deterioration in the faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.
note: Ageing body, accepting decline, sickness and death

tags.when_helps: Someone noticing their body ageing, naming plainly that youth, health and life all lead to decline.

text: Curse this wretched old age, which makes you so ugly. That’s how much this delightful puppet is ground down by old age. Even if you live for a hundred years, you’ll still end up dying. Death spares no one, but crushes all underfoot.
note: Frustration at growing old; mortality comes to all

tags.when_helps: Someone angry at ageing, voicing that frustration and the hard truth that death spares no one.

text: When a noble disciple has tried again and again, recollected again and again, entered immersion again and again, and understood with wisdom again and again, they will be confident of this: ‘I have previously heard of these things. But now I have direct meditative experience of them, and see them with penetrating wisdom.’
note: Persistent practice turns borrowed belief into lived knowing

tags.when_helps: Someone persisting in a practice who wants assurance that repeated effort turns teaching into direct experience.

text: Mendicants, there are these four right efforts. What four? It’s when a mendicant generates enthusiasm, tries, makes an effort, exerts the mind, and strives so that bad, unskillful qualities don’t arise. They generate enthusiasm, try, make an effort, exert the mind, and strive so that bad, unskillful qualities that have arisen are given up. They generate enthusiasm, try, make an effort, exert the mind, and strive so that skillful qualities arise. They generate enthusiasm, try, make an effort, exert the mind, and strive so that skillful qualities that have arisen remain, are not lost, but increase, mature, and are fully developed. These are the four right efforts.
note: Effort to drop bad habits and grow good ones

tags.when_helps: Someone wanting a clear framework for self-improvement: prevent and drop the bad, grow and keep the good.

text: And what is enthusiasm that’s too lax? It’s when enthusiasm is coupled with laziness. This is called lax enthusiasm. And what is enthusiasm that’s too tense? It’s when enthusiasm is coupled with restlessness. This is called tense enthusiasm.
note: Balancing effort between laziness and restless overdrive

tags.when_helps: Someone either slacking or straining too hard, naming the balance between lazy and tense effort.

text: “What meditation does Venerable Anuruddha practice so that physical pain doesn’t occupy his mind?” “Reverends, I meditate with my mind firmly established in the four kinds of mindfulness meditation so that physical pain doesn’t occupy my mind. What four? I meditate observing an aspect of the body … feelings … mind … principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world. I meditate with my mind firmly established in these four kinds of mindfulness meditation so that physical pain doesn’t occupy my mind.”
note: Serious illness; keeping physical pain from overwhelming the mind

tags.when_helps: Someone gravely ill or in pain, offering mindfulness as a way to keep pain from filling the mind.

text: And how is mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated to be very fruitful and beneficial? It’s when a mendicant—gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut—sits down cross-legged, sets their body straight, and brings mindfulness to the present. Just mindful, they breathe in. Mindful, they breathe out. Breathing in heavily they know: ‘I’m breathing in heavily.’ Breathing out heavily they know: ‘I’m breathing out heavily.’ Breathing in lightly they know: ‘I’m breathing in lightly.’ Breathing out lightly they know: ‘I’m breathing out lightly.’
note: Calming the mind by simply noticing the breath

tags.when_helps: Someone anxious or scattered who wants simple instructions to sit and follow the breath.

display: SN 54.8, The Simile of the Lamp
text: Suppose an oil lamp depended on oil and a wick to burn. As the oil and the wick are used up, it would be extinguished due to not being fed. In the same way, feeling the end of the body draw close, they understand: ‘I feel the end of the body draw close.’ Feeling the end of life draw close, they understand: ‘I feel the end of life draw close.’ They understand: ‘When my body breaks up and my life has come to an end, everything that’s felt, since I no longer take pleasure in it, will become cool right here.’
note: Facing the end of life with calm awareness

tags.when_helps: Someone facing the end of life seeking a calm, clear way to understand the body and life drawing to a close.

text: In the last month of summer, when the dust and dirt is stirred up, a large storm out of season disperses and settles it on the spot. In the same way, when this immersion due to mindfulness of breathing is developed and cultivated it’s peaceful and sublime, a delectable and blissful meditation. And it disperses and settles unskillful qualities on the spot whenever they arise.
note: Breathing meditation settling an agitated, stirred-up mind

tags.when_helps: Someone with a stirred-up mind, showing how breath meditation settles it like rain settling dust.

display: SN 55.2, The Objective of the Spiritual Life
text: “Those who have faith and ethics, confidence, and vision of the truth, in time arrive at happiness, the objective of the spiritual life.”
note: Patience on the path; integrity leads to happiness

tags.when_helps: Someone on a spiritual path wondering if it leads anywhere, promising happiness in time.

display: SN 55.7, The People of Bamboo Gate
text: And what is the explanation of the Dhamma that applies to oneself? It’s when a noble disciple reflects: ‘I want to live and don’t want to die; I want to be happy and recoil from pain. Since this is so, if someone were to take my life, I wouldn’t like that. But others also want to live and don’t want to die; they want to be happy and recoil from pain. So if I were to take the life of someone else, they wouldn’t like that either. The thing that is disliked by me is also disliked by others. Since I dislike this thing, how can I inflict it on someone else?’
note: Empathy: others want happiness just as I do

situations: conflict with a friend or colleague
tags.when_helps: Someone tempted to hurt another, inviting them to see that others want to live and be happy just as they do.

text: Suppose a person was to sink a pot of ghee or oil into a deep lake and break it open. Its shards and chips would sink down, while the ghee or oil in it would rise up, headed for a higher place. In the same way, take someone whose mind has for a long time been imbued with faith, ethics, learning, generosity, and wisdom. Their body is formed, made up of the four principal states, produced by mother and father, built up from rice and porridge, liable to impermanence, to wearing away and erosion, to breaking up and destruction. Right here the crows, vultures, hawks, hounds, jackals, and many kinds of little creatures devour it. But their mind rises up, headed for a higher place.
note: Fear of dying; a good life outlasts the body

keywords: ghee rising from a broken pot
tags.when_helps: Someone afraid of what happens at death, offering the image of a well-lived mind rising like oil from a broken pot.

text: Whoever has faith in the Realized One, unwavering and well grounded; whose ethical conduct is good, praised and loved by the noble ones; who has confidence in the Saṅgha, and correct view: they’re said to be prosperous, their life is not in vain. So let the wise devote themselves to faith, ethical behaviour, confidence, and insight into the teaching, remembering the instructions of the Buddhas.
note: A life not in vain; true prosperity through faith and conduct

tags.when_helps: A Buddhist reader fearing their life is wasted, affirming that faith, ethics and insight make a life not in vain.

text: When they live diligently, joy springs up. Being joyful, rapture springs up. When the mind is full of rapture, the body becomes tranquil. When the body is tranquil, they feel bliss. And when blissful, the mind becomes immersed in samādhi. When the mind is immersed in samādhi, principles become clear.
note: Steady effort in practice brings joy, calm and clarity

tags.when_helps: Someone feeling glad in their practice, tracing how joy deepens into tranquillity, bliss and clarity.

text: “One who desires merit, grounded in the skillful, develops the path to realize freedom from death. Once they’ve reached the heart of the teaching, <j>delighting in ending, they don’t tremble at the approach <j>of the King of Death.”
note: Facing death without fear through a grounded spiritual path

tags.safety_reason: Read alone, 'delighting in ending' and not trembling at Death can read as delighting in death itself.
tags.when_helps: A practitioner afraid of death, suggesting that one grounded in the teaching need not tremble as death approaches.

text: Mendicants, don’t think bad, unskillful thoughts, such as sensual, malicious, and cruel thoughts. Why is that? Because those thoughts aren’t beneficial or relevant to the fundamentals of the spiritual life. They don’t lead to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment.
note: Letting go of malicious and cruel thoughts

tags.when_helps: Someone indulging cruel or lustful thoughts, reminding them such thoughts lead nowhere good.

text: Mendicants, don’t get into arguments, such as: ‘You don’t understand this teaching and training. I understand this teaching and training. What, you understand this teaching and training? You’re practicing wrong. I’m practicing right. I stay on topic, you don’t. You said last what you should have said first. You said first what you should have said last. What you’ve thought so much about has been disproved. Your doctrine is refuted. Go on, save your doctrine! You’re trapped; get yourself out of this—if you can!’ Why is that? Because those discussions aren’t beneficial or relevant to the fundamentals of the spiritual life. They don’t lead to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment.
note: The futility of point-scoring arguments

situations: conflict with a friend or colleague
tags.when_helps: Someone caught up in point-scoring arguments, showing how pointless that kind of dispute is.

display: SN 56.11, Rolling Forth the Wheel of Dhamma
text: Mendicants, these two extremes should not be cultivated by one gone forth. What two? Indulgence in sensual pleasures, which is low, crude, ordinary, ignoble, and pointless. And indulgence in self-mortification, which is painful, ignoble, and pointless. Avoiding these two extremes, the Realized One understood the middle way of practice, which gives vision and knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, awakening, and extinguishment.
note: Finding the middle way between indulgence and self-punishment

tags.when_helps: Someone swinging between indulgence and harsh self-denial, pointing to a balanced middle way.

display: SN 56.11, Rolling Forth the Wheel of Dhamma
text: Now this is the noble truth of suffering. Rebirth is suffering; old age is suffering; illness is suffering; death is suffering; being coupled with the disliked is suffering; separation from the liked is suffering; not getting what you wish for is suffering.
note: Naming the suffering of illness, loss and unmet wishes

tags.when_helps: Someone hurting from loss, illness or unmet wishes, naming these honestly as the shared suffering of life.

text: Then the Buddha picked up a few rosewood leaves in his hand and addressed the mendicants: “What do you think, mendicants? Which is more: the few leaves in my hand, or those in the grove above?” “Sir, the few leaves in your hand are a tiny amount. There are far more leaves in the grove above.” “In the same way, there is much more that I have directly known but have not explained to you. What I have explained is a tiny amount. And why haven’t I explained it? Because it’s not beneficial or relevant to the fundamentals of the spiritual life.
note: Focusing on what truly helps rather than knowing everything

tags.when_helps: Someone overwhelmed by endless questions, inviting focus on the few things that truly help.

text: Suppose there was an iron pillar or an Indra’s pillar with deep foundations, firmly embedded, imperturbable and unshakable. Even if violent storms were to blow up out of the east, the west, the north, and the south, they couldn’t make it shake or rock or tremble. Why is that? It’s because that Indra’s pillar is firmly embedded, with deep foundations. In the same way, there are ascetics and brahmins who truly understand about suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. They don’t gaze up at the face of another ascetic or brahmin, thinking: ‘Surely this worthy one knows and sees.’
note: Steadiness from deep understanding, not leaning on others

tags.when_helps: Someone who keeps looking to others for answers, showing the steadiness of one who understands for themselves.
